units.translation: No one of the gods is angry on my behalf.
I am set as a wakeful guard of the land on behalf of those who sleep.
And over the Gorgopian lake the light flashed.
And over the sea and the sea-girt cities.
And over the sea — they came.
Of houses teeming with abundance, beyond what is best.
Neither overstepping nor falling short of the due measure of grace.
They utter boastful words against the city.
But she must pass over the star-neighboring peaks and go to the midday path.
To pass over the headland that looks down upon the Saronic strait.
He will find a flame stronger than lightning and a mighty thunderclap surpassing thunder (thus Blomfield for βροντάς).
For this misfortune surpasses the ability either to speak or to ask about the sufferings.
where, since the words placed in the strophic verse do not correspond accurately, Meineke in Philologus vol. 19 p. 207 conjectured ὑπέρβριθυς ἐπεμπίτνων [exceedingly heavy, falling upon].
A deity exceedingly heavy falling upon,
where Weilius reads ὑπερτερώτερα [more surpassing]: see under ὑπέρτερος [higher].
These are the griefs at the hearths in the houses, and there are things even more surpassing than these,

where τύχη ὑπερβόρεος [Hyperborean fortune] signifies the highest happiness, such as that of the Hyperboreans, who were believed to live longer and more blessedly than other mortals: see Pomponius Mela 3, 5, 2 with the note of Tzschucke.
You speak of things greater than great fortune and Hyperborean fortune,
And the exceedingly old man walks the threefold paths.
(perfect of the unused present δείδω) I fear for someone.
As a dove that feeds all her young fears greatly for her children in the nest, the serpent that brings restless sleep.
Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 68, 24 explains ὑπερδικεῖν [to plead for] as ὑπέρ τινος εἰπεῖν δίκην [to speak justice on behalf of someone].
For how do you plead the cause of this man's exile?
to speak justice on behalf of someone
These things would be justly done, nay, exceedingly justly.
of gods who have care for human affairs. See similar things in the Thesaurus vol. 8 p. 200.
That not by strength nor by force should he prevail, but by guile to overcome those who are superior.
Surpassing all mortals in wealth, he is fortunate in his lot.
Where they might hold the city's strength superior.
And holding a cloud over, with a snowstorm of rounded stones he will make the land shadowed.
Hyperenor, among the survivors of the sown men in the battle against Cadmus, is mentioned from Aeschylus (fr. 385) by the scholiast on Euripides' Phoenissae 942.
the survivors of the sown men in the battle against Cadmus
